text: Every model in this course, from the humble straight line to a large language model, is trained by the same short loop. Make a prediction, measure how wrong it is, work out which way to nudge each parameter, nudge it, and go again. The details change from model to model, but once you can write this loop from memory, you can train almost anything.

The loop begins with the forward pass. A mini-batch of inputs flows through the model, layer by layer, and comes out as predictions. The loss function then compares those predictions with the true targets and boils the whole batch down to a single number, an average of how wrong the model was. Everything that follows exists to make that one number smaller.

The backward pass answers a precise question: if I nudged this one parameter slightly, how much would the loss change? That rate is the gradient, and backpropagation computes it for every parameter at once, by running the chain rule from the loss back through each layer. The result is one gradient for every weight, with exactly the same shape as the weight itself.

Then comes the update. Each weight steps a little against its gradient: the new weight is the old weight minus the learning rate times the gradient, because the gradient points uphill and we want to go down. Frameworks such as PyTorch add gradients into a running total by default, so the old gradients must be cleared before each backward pass; forget that, and every step is pushed by the ghosts of earlier batches.

These steps repeat over the data. One step handles one mini-batch, and once every example has been seen, we have completed an epoch. At the start of each epoch we shuffle the data, so the batches mix differently every time and the model cannot learn anything from the order. Small datasets may need many epochs, while the largest models see most of their data only about once.

A careful loop also keeps records. It logs the training loss as it goes, and every so often it pauses learning to measure the loss on a validation set, with no updates at all, so that we can see whether the model is truly improving or just memorising. It saves checkpoints of the weights, so a crash or a bad turn does not cost the whole run, and so we can keep the version that did best on validation.

Pretraining a large language model is this very loop. The inputs are batches of text, the targets are the same text shifted by one token, the loss is cross-entropy over the next token, and the loop runs for tens or hundreds of thousands of steps across many machines. Next, we learn to read the loss curve this loop produces.
